Article Title: After announcing biggest layoffs in Volkswagen's history, CEO of Europe's biggest car company makes ‘China request’ to EU, similar to what Ford CEO Jim Farley warned US about
Article Text:
Volkswagen CEO's 'China warning' to European Union

Rapid growth of Chinese car companies in Europe

Volkswagen chief executive officer (CEO) Oliver Blume has called on European policymakers to establish the necessary regulatory framework to ensure the German automaker’s sweeping restructuring succeeds. According to a report by Reuters, addressing an event dubbed "For Europe" on the sidelines of the Paris motor show, Blume asked the European Union to make efforts to shield domestic industry from low-cost Chinese rivals.Blume framed the turnaround as a collective duty, arguing that while corporations must sharpen their competitive edge and generate attractive business prospects, public officials are equally responsible for laying down viable operating conditions. "This is a shared responsibility: The business community must become more ⁠competitive and create attractive opportunities, while policymakers must establish the right framework conditions," he said.His views echo with that of Ford CEO Jim Farley who recently said that the US must carefully weigh how and whether Chinese automakers should enter ​the American market, and pointed to Europe as aThe remarks come at a time when Europe’s largest car manufacturer is undergoing the biggest-ever restructuring in its history.Volkswagen is cutting thousands of jobs and considering factory closures to slash costs. Earlier this year, the company announced a total of 100,000 layoffs; biggest in the group's 89-year history.Blume is also grappling with mounting pressure from shareholders to demonstrate that his strategic blueprint extends past cost reduction to substantive advancements in vehicle software and development, amid union pushback against deep head-count reductions and potential closures affecting up to four German manufacturing plants.The European Union imposed tariffs on Chinese-made fully electric cars two years ago, but Chinese automakers have responded by ​expanding into combustion-engine models and plug-in hybrids. Chinese brands reportedly made up for more than 26% of the Western European plug-in hybrid market in the second quarter, up from just ​2.2% in the same period two years earlier.A record 20 Chinese car brands are expected at the upcoming Paris Motor Show, underscoring how rapidly China's automakers have established themselves as ​a competitive threat in Europe.Although Volkswagen maintains a roughly 25% share of the European market, rapid inroads made by Chinese brands have rattled industry executives.Blume is among prominent German automotive figures seeking firmer European Union intervention, as broader industry anxiety shifts from the threat of Chinese trade retaliation to the fallout of aggressive overseas discounting spilling directly onto European roads.
Article Summary: Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume has called on European policymakers to establish the necessary regulatory framework to ensure the German automaker’s sweeping restructuring succeeds. Blume framed the turnaround as a collective duty, arguing that while corporations must sharpen their competitive edge and generate attractive business prospects, public officials are equally responsible.

Article Title: SBI warns customers of rise in Jumped Deposit Scam, here's what it is and his to stay safe
Article Text:
What is the Jumped Deposit Scam and how it works

SBI's advice to users

State Bank of India (SBI) has alerted the customers about the increasing online fraud known as the ‘Jumped Deposit Scam’. SBI has asked the customers to not trust unexpected credits received in their bank accounts and to remain cautious of suspicious payment requests. As part of the National Cyber Security Special Campaign 6.0, the country’s largest bank said that the fraudsters are using small deposits to gain the trust of victims before attempting to steal larger amounts via UPI payment requests. “Beware of Jumped Deposit Scam! In a Jumped Deposit Scam, scammers claim to have "accidentally" credited a small amount to your account to win your trust. When you try to return it, they trick you into approving a high-value payment request,” wrote SBI in a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter).According to SBI, the scam begins when fraudsters claim to have “accidentally” transferred a small amount of money into a customer's bank account. The scammer then contacts the victim and requests that the money be returned.However, instead of asking for a simple transfer, the fraudster sends a payment collect request or another transaction request designed to trick the victim into authorising a much larger amount than the original deposit.“Unexpected credit in your account? It's a trap!” SBI said in a post shared on social media, cautioning customers against acting on such requests without verification.The bank said scammers often use emotional manipulation, urgency, or emergency situations to pressure victims into approving transactions quickly. By first depositing a small amount, fraudsters attempt to make their story appear genuine and lower the victim's guard. Once the victim approves a payment request, the money is transferred out of their account, resulting in financial loss.The bank listed three precautions:* Block and report: Block the number immediately and report the incident to the bank on priority.* Resist pressure: Don't give in to emotional blackmail or emergency UPI requests without confirming them first.* Check the caller: Always respond to calls that begin with the prefix 1600. SBI says these are genuine and secure calls from the bank.Apart from this, it is also advisable to never approve any payment request that you didn't start yourself. Also, if you see a credit you can't explain, don't send anything back yourself. Contact your bank through its official number or branch and let it handle the reversal.
Article Summary: State Bank of India (SBI) has alerted the customers about the increasing online fraud known as the ‘Jumped Deposit Scam’ SBI has asked the customers to not trust unexpected credits received in their bank accounts and to remain cautious of suspicious payment requests. The bank said scammers often use emotional manipulation, urgency, or emergency situations to pressure victims into approving transactions quickly.

Article Text:
How Google Maps can help you save fuel and money with these easy steps

Drivers across United Kingdom (UK) can now check real-time gas station prices on Google Maps. This comes after the UK government announced partnership with search giant Google . AS per the release, drivers are set to save at the pump as near real-time petrol and diesel prices now appear on Google Maps. To checking local fuel prices, users need to open Google Maps and search for a forecourt nearby, with near real time prices for petrol and diesel displayed on the app.As per the official release, this marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, giving families some breathing space with the cost of living.Minister for Energy Consumers Polly Billington said, "Tackling the affordability crisis is our first responsibility and for so many families and businesses, petrol and diesel are essential goods, not luxuries. Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a gamechanger for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers to find the best deal and save money at the pump. "Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said, "Getting the best price at the pump is now easier. This doesn’t fix everything; bills have gone up because of events in the Middle East. But we’re not powerless.And small changes like this, cutting tax on electricity bills and capping bus fares at £2 all help give families a bit of breathing space."What is UK government's Fuel Finder schemeUK Government claims that Fuel Finder scheme was created to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices following a recommendation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). It added that an overwhelming majority of petrol stations are inputting data to Fuel Finder promptly, with around 99% of all fuel sold on UK roads now reflected.Since February, it has been compulsory for petrol stations across the UK to report the price of their fuel within 30 minutes of it changing or risk a fine – and the CMA can take action where there is evidence that petrol stations are not complying with the law.The data is already used by thousands of drivers across apps such as Waze, Petrol Prices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch, and its integration with Google Maps will help millions more motorists find the best price at the pump.Sarah-Jayne Williams, Director of Global Product Partnerships for Geo at Google, said, "Navigating fuel rising costs shouldn’t add stress to everyday journeys. Integrating Fuel Finder data into Google Maps and Waze gives drivers visibility on nearby pump prices, helping drivers make intentional choices to help their budgets go further this winter."
Article Summary: Near real-time petrol and diesel prices now appear on Google Maps. Users need to open Google Maps and search for a forecourt nearby. This marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares.

Article Title: As US suspends Green card programme for Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL; Shark Tank India judge Anupam Mittal remembers 'Full Emotional Atyachar' he faced when he went to return his Green Card years ago
Article Text:
Anupam Mittal recalls his own Green Card dilemma

'The officer looked at me like I was crazy'

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you consider giving up a foreign residency status for opportunities in your own country? Yes, I would No, I prefer living abroad 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Read Anupam Mittal’s complete post here

Like most ambitious Indian kids, I dreamt of life in America.

And I got there! Great education & job. More money than I had imagined.

Within four years, I was a multimillionaire living the American dream.

Then came the Green Card. I was ecstatic.

But somehow the feeling was fleeting.

So in 2004, I came back to India to build.

But every year, I still flew back to the US to give 'hazri' & I struggled with the feeling.

So I went to the consulate in Mumbai to surrender the Green Card.

The officer looked at me like I was crazy.

“Think about this. Once you give it up, you may never get it back.”

Full emotional atyachar - walked out with it still in my pocket

A year later, I went back.

This time, I handed it over.

And I walked out feeling lighter than I had in years.

For the first time, both my feet were on the same side.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I had stayed.

I probably would have been a wealthy VP at a tech company, eating once a week at an Indian restaurant worrying that AI would take my job.

I would not have built the companies I did, backed 300+ Indian startups, or sat on @sharktank India watching new Indian founders dream bigger than we ever did.

Which is why I look at the H-1B and Green Card turmoil in America differently.

For decades, success meant a life in the USA. That story is finally breaking.

And I think that's a very good thing

The time is here to build global tech & brand companies from India.

Sometimes a closing door is what makes you realize where home is.

As the US suspends a key green card step for several major Indian IT firms, entrepreneur and Shark Tank India judge and Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal has shared how he gave up his own green card, and why he sees America's immigration turmoil as an opportunity for India. Recently, the US government suspended several major technology and outsourcing firms, including Infosys Wipro , HCL Technologies , Cognizant and Capgemini, from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme (PERM), a key route used by employers to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards. The action also affects Microsoft and Adobe, with US authorities stating that they will neither accept new applications nor process pending labour certification requests involving the companies.The move has raised concerns among thousands of foreign workers, particularly Indians employed in the US technology sector. While the suspension does not affect existing H-1B visas, it could delay or block one of the most important pathways to permanent residency in the United States.In a post shared on professional networking platform LinkedIn, Mittal shared a personal story about giving up his own Green Card years ago.Mittal said that, like many ambitious young Indians, he had once dreamed of building a life in America. He said he achieved that goal through a strong education, a successful job and financial success, becoming a multimillionaire within a few years."Within four years, I was a multimillionaire living the American dream. Then came the Green Card. I was ecstatic. But somehow the feeling was fleeting," he wrote. Mittal said that despite receiving permanent residency, he decided to move back to India in 2004 to build companies. However, he continued travelling to the US every year to maintain his residency status, even as he struggled with whether he should hold on to the Green Card.The entrepreneur recounted visiting the US consulate in Mumbai to surrender the document. According to Mittal, the consular officer was surprised by his decision and urged him to reconsider."The officer looked at me like I was crazy. 'Think about this. Once you give it up, you may never get it back'," Mittal wrote. He jokingly described the exchange as "full emotional atyachar", adding that he ultimately walked out of the office with the Green Card still in his pocket.A year later, however, he returned and completed the process. "This time, I handed it over. And I walked out feeling lighter than I had in years. For the first time, both my feet were on the same side," he said.Mittal used the story to reflect on changing attitudes among Indian entrepreneurs and professionals. He said that had he remained in the United States, he might have become a wealthy technology executive. Instead, returning to India allowed him to build companies, invest in more than 300 startups and become part of the country's growing startup ecosystem.🇮🇳
Article Summary: Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal shares his story of giving up his Green Card. Mittal said he had once dreamed of building a life in America. He said he achieved that goal through a strong education, a successful job and financial success.

Article Title: Robert E Hall, Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for macroeconomic stabilisation models
Article Text:
Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford won in the Economic Sciences category for 2026

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford for their contributions to understanding macroeconomic stabilisation, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Monday. The two economists were recognised “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.”"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs," said the Academy in its press release.Robert E Hall earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of California, Berkeley, and a PhD in economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), while Michael Woodford holds a bachelor’s degree from the University of Chicago, a law degree from Yale Law School and a PhD in economics from MIT.They both were recognised for developing economic models that have helped governments and central banks better manage economic fluctuations. Their work showed how timely changes in interest rates, government spending and taxation could help reduce the impact of recessions and prevent economies from overheating.Their research helped address the limitations of earlier economic models, particularly those exposed during the oil crises of the 1970s, when high inflation, unemployment and weak growth occurred simultaneously.Instead of relying mainly on broad economic indicators such as inflation, production and consumption, the two economists developed models based on how individual households and businesses make financial decisions.A key finding of their work was that people and businesses make decisions based not only on current economic conditions but also on their expectations of the future. This showed how governments and central banks could influence economic activity by clearly communicating their policy plans. Their models have since become important tools for designing monetary and fiscal policies and responding to economic shocks.“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.Unlike the other Nobel Prizes, the Economics Prize was not established by Alfred Nobel in his will. It was instituted in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank, Sweden’s central bank, to mark its 300th anniversary, and was first awarded in 1969 to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen. Officially known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, it is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences under the same principles as the original Nobel Prizes. The prize money is funded by Sweden’s central bank and is equal to that awarded in the other Nobel categories. Meanwhile, two Indian-born economists have won the prize in this category. Amartya Sen won in 1998 for his contributions to welfare economics, and Abhijit Banerjee in 2019, who shared the award with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.
Article Summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford. The two economists were recognised “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation’ Their work showed how timely changes in interest rates, government spending and taxation could help reduce the impact of recessions and prevent economies from overheating.

Article Title: Direct selling in India is now a Rs 23,522-crore business with 91 lakh sellers: ADSEI report
Article Text:
The industry has grown from Rs 16,776 crore in 2019-20, a compound annual growth rate of about 7%.

India's Direct Selling Industry: Market size & Growth

India's Direct Selling Industry At a Glance

India's direct selling industry clocked sales of Rs 23,522 crore in 2024-25 and is set to cross Rs 25,000 crore in the current fiscal, according to a report released on Monday at Bharat Mandapam by the Association of Direct Selling Entities of India (ADSEI) and its research partner Kantar.The industry has grown from Rs 16,776 crore in 2019-20, a compound annual growth rate of about 7%, while the number of active direct sellers rose from 72 lakh to 91 lakh over the same period. Women make up 47% of them, or roughly 43 lakh sellers. The report places India 11th among the world's top 15 direct selling markets, worth an estimated $2.8-3 billion.ADSEI president Dr Sanjeev Kumar said the report established "with credible quantified and qualitative data" what the sector contributes, chiefly "livelihoods for more than 91 lakh people, nearly half of them women".Wellness products alone account for about 61% of sales; add cosmetics and personal care, and the share rises to 86%.Maharashtra is the largest market at Rs 3,058 crore, followed by West Bengal (Rs 2,376 crore) and Uttar Pradesh (Rs 1,788 crore). The top 10 states together contribute about 70% of national sales.A survey of 572 sellers conducted for the report found that 65% depend on direct selling as their only source of income, and 73% described their month-on-month earnings as very or somewhat consistent.Those with other sources of income reported average additional earnings of about Rs 18,000 a month. Some 69% of sellers are between 25 and 44 years old."Behind the Rs 23,522 crore are 91 lakh Indians who decided to bet on themselves," said Gautam Bali, patron, ADSEI. "But too many still leave before their business finds its feet. Sharper training, stronger governance and an uncompromising commitment to the consumer are how we ensure that everyone who joins with hope stays to build something lasting."The report credits the Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules, 2021 with formalising the sector, and 83% of sellers surveyed viewed the impact of policy favourably. Their wish list for the government includes easier access to bank accounts and loans (61%), uniform central regulation across states (53%) and a dedicated regulator along the lines of Sebi or Irdai (42%).The numbers also show how far the industry has to go. Per-capita spending on direct selling in India is about $2, against $8-12 in the lower rungs of the global top 10. Breaking into that group would require the market to reach $6-7 billion, growing 12-14% a year, nearly twice its current pace. The business is also concentrated: six companies with revenue of Rs 1,000 crore or more hold about 68% of industry revenue, while over 400 firms earn less than Rs 10 crore each.Puneet Avasthi, director at Kantar, said the industry was "transitioning from a participation-led growth model to one increasingly driven by productivity, value creation, and ecosystem maturity"
Article Summary: India's direct selling industry clocked sales of Rs 23,522 crore in 2024-25. The industry has grown from Rs 16,776 crore in 2019-20, a compound annual growth rate of about 7%. The number of active direct sellers rose from 72 lakh to 91 lakh over the same period.

Article Title: 3km, 12km, 21km: How far are Delhi’s new protest sites from Jantar Mantar?
Article Text:
Delhi Police has officially shifted protest activities away from Jantar Mantar

Ramlila Maidan: Around 3km from Jantar Mantar

CBD Ground, East Delhi: Around 12km away

Burari Ground: Around 21 km from Jantar Mantar

Why has Delhi Police changed the designated protest sites?





NEW DELHI: With Delhi Police removing Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest venues and shifting demonstrations to three alternative grounds, protesters may now have to travel farther from the capital’s political centre to stage a dharna.Ramlila Maidan, CBD Ground in East Delhi and Burari Ground have been named as the new venues, located around 3km, 10–12km and21 km from Jantar Mantar, respectively.The decision marks a change in Delhi’s long-standing arrangement for public demonstrations at Jantar Mantar, a prominent site for political protests and public campaigns.The new locations are spread across central, east and outer Delhi.Ramlila Maidan is the closest of the three newly designated protest venues, at an estimated distance of around 3km from Jantar Mantar.Located in central Delhi, the ground has hosted large public gatherings, political rallies and demonstrations over the years.Its proximity to central Delhi makes it a key alternative for protesters who want to assemble relatively close to the city’s administrative and political hubs.CBD Ground in East Delhi is around 12km from Jantar Mantar. Its location shifts demonstrations towards the eastern part of the capital, away from the central area where Jantar Mantar has traditionally served as a protest venue.The ground is among the three locations identified by Delhi Police as alternatives for demonstrations. The distance could be a consideration for protesters travelling from central and other parts of the city.At approximately 21km from Jantar Mantar, Burari Ground is the farthest of the three alternative sites listed. Located in north Delhi, it has been used for large public gatherings and is designated as a venue for demonstrations.For protesters who previously assembled at Jantar Mantar, travelling to Burari could mean a longer journey, depending on their starting point and route.Delhi Police’s decision to remove Jantar Mantar as a designated protest venue follows discussions on identifying alternative locations for demonstrations.The move comes amid recent protests in the capital over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.According to Standing Order No. 48/2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) had constituted a committee to examine alternative venues where citizens could exercise their right to organise protests and demonstrations.Based on the committee’s recommendations, Jantar Mantar has been removed from the list of designated protest venues, while the three locations have been designated for holding demonstrations.The police have identified the three grounds as replacements, with revised standard operating procedures for demonstrations expected to clarify the arrangements.The change does not, by itself, amount to a blanket ban on peaceful protests in Delhi.However, organisers will need to follow the applicable permission requirements and procedures for the newly designated venues.(With agency inputs)
Article Summary: Ramlila Maidan, CBD Ground in East Delhi and Burari Ground have been named as the new venues. The new locations are spread across central, east and outer Delhi. The decision marks a change in Delhi’s long-standing arrangement for public demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.

Article Title: Mumbai needs 57% more water by 2041; many key plans on paper
Article Text:
Mumbai is expected to encounter a 10% water cut that may persist until 2027 due to insufficient rainfall.

The city's daily water demand is projected to rise significantly by 2041, reaching 6,424 million litres.





MUMBAI: At a time the city is likely to face a 10% water cut for the rest of this year and well into 2027, data from the BMC's hydraulic engineering department highlights the urgency of developing new water sources to meet the city's growing demand and ensure long-term water security.Mumbai receives 4,100 million litres of water per day (MLD) from the BMC's seven lakes and dams. However, the lakes failed to reach 100% of their capacity by the end of the monsoon this year, owing to deficient rainfall in Aug and Sept.The BMC's recently published Environment Status Report 2025-26 projects the city's daily water demand to rise to 6,424 MLD by 2041, up from the current supply of 4,100 MLD. A senior civic official said demand already stands at around 4,600 MLD, leaving a shortfall that the existing sources cannot bridge.The BMC has identified six new water sources that are expected to add a combined 3,303 MLD to the city's supply. Three major projects -- Gargai, Pinjal and the inter-state Damanganga-Pinjal project -- account for 2,891 MLD, or nearly 88% of the proposed additional supply.The Gargai project, expected to yield 440 MLD, is under way, with completion targeted for 2029. The Pinjal project, planned to supply 865 MLD, is still at the planning stage, while the Damanganga-Pinjal project, which is expected to contribute 1,586 MLD, remains on paper.The latter requires coordination between the Centre and the govts of Maharashtra and Gujarat.The BMC has also proposed desalination plants at Manori and Versova, each with a capacity of 200 MLD, and a 12 MLD advanced tertiary treatment plant at Colaba. Preliminary work on the proposed Manori desalination plant has begun.The status of the projects came into focus during a visit by ruling BJP leaders in the BMC, including mayor Ritu Tawde and standing committee chairman Prabhakar Shinde, to the civic body's Tansa and Modak Sagar lakes. During the visit, the leaders sought details from hydraulic engineering department officials on measures to expedite the long-pending Pinjal and Damanganga-Pinjal projects.A senior hydraulic engineering department official said, "Several major projects have been identified, and work on some is under way to augment the city's supply. Mumbai's population is steadily increasing, and daily demand is projected to reach 6,424 MLD by 2041, including losses during transit and distribution."
Article Summary: Mumbai is expected to encounter a 10% water cut that may persist until 2027. The city's daily water demand is projected to rise significantly by 2041, reaching 6,424 million litres. Three major projects -- Gargai, Pinjal and the inter-state Damanganga-Pinjal project -- account for 2,891 MLD.

Article Title: Mumbai is already thirsty: Why the 2041 problem is really a 2026 problem
Article Text:
By 2041, Mumbai’s demand is projected to be 56.7% higher than the existing supply of 4,100 MLD.

Mumbai’s water gap

Demand has already outpaced supply

Three projects hold key to future

Mumbai’s search for new water sources

The key is three big projects

Desalination is an alternative, but not a quick fix

The real test is in execution





MUMBAI: Mumbai’s water crisis is not a problem to be pushed to the next decade. The city is already struggling with water scarcity, facing a 10% water cut and increasingly unpredictable monsoons, even as its demand is expected to soar 57% by 2041. The warning is stark: The infrastructure to ensure Mumbai’s future water supply is not keeping pace with the urgency of today.Mumbai gets some 4,100 million liters of water per day (MLD) from seven lakes and dams, but its actual daily requirement is estimated at some 4,600-4,665 MLD, leaving a deficit of more than 500 MLD. The BMC’s environment status report 2025-26 expects demand to reach 6,424 MLD by 2041.That would leave a gap of 2,324 MLD against today’s supply, even without taking into account the challenge of sourcing additional sources and efficiently distributing water.The immediate crisis shows the vulnerability. Mumbai’s reservoirs did not fill to their full capacity by the end of the monsoon this year after deficient rainfall in August and September.In June, the water levels in the seven lakes dropped to less than 10% of their total capacity, and the BMC imposed stringent restrictions.By September, the stocks had recovered to around 96% but the civic administration went ahead with the 10% cut. The Maharashtra government has also ordered a minimum 10% cut in water supply in urban and rural areas from October 16 in view of the drought-like conditions.The BMC has identified six more sources which are expected to contribute 3,303 MLD in total. Three projects – Gargai, Pinjal and Damanganga-Pinjal inter-state scheme – constitute 2,891 MLD, or about 88% of the proposed augmentation. But their progress illustrates how much more is required to get water from a source to household taps.Gargai, expected to supply 440 MLD, is under construction and is expected to be completed by 2029. The Pinjal, which is to contribute 865 MLD, is still in the planning stage while the 1,586 MLD Damanganga-Pinjal project is still on paper.This requires coordination between the Center and Maharashtra and Gujarat governments. The delays in these projects are important as Mumbai is unable to depend only on the seven existing reservoirs to bridge the growing supply gap.In addition, the BMC is also building two desalination plants at Manori and Versova with each having a capacity of 200 MLD and a 12 MLD advanced tertiary treatment plant at Colaba. Initial work on Manori has been started and the project is expected to add to the city’s sources apart from rain-dependent reservoirs. But even the first 200 MLD from Manori would only be a part of the present deficit of over 500 MLD.The issue came to the fore during a visit by mayor Ritu Tawde, standing committee chairman Prabhakar Shinde and other ruling BJP leaders to Tansa and Modak Sagar lakes. They pressed hydraulic engineering officials for details to speed up Pinjal and Damanganga-Pinjal. The challenge is not just announcing new sources but getting clearances, coordinating across governments and completing projects on time.By 2041, Mumbai’s demand is projected to be 56.7% higher than the existing supply of 4,100 MLD. But already, the city is short of water today.Unless long-pending projects shift from plans to reliable supply, the 2041 deadline risks becoming a false comfort: Mumbai will not suddenly face a water crisis in 2041. It is already facing the conditions that make one inevitable.
Article Summary: By 2041, Mumbai’s demand is projected to be 56.7% higher than the existing supply of 4,100 MLD. Three projects – Gargai, Pinjal and Damanganga-Pinjal inter-state scheme – constitute 2,891 MLD, or about 88% of the proposed augmentation.

Article Title: Pregnant woman with dengue fails to get hospital bed in Mumbai
Article Text:
Mumbai recorded 1,378 cases of dengue in Sept

Mumbai:





Official data may show a dip in Mumbai’s dengue cases compared to last year, but that brings little comfort to severely ill patients rushing to hospitals. Doctors report that many of those admitted have critically low platelet counts.For instance, 29-year-old Manisha Rajak, who is 6 to 7 months pregnant, was rushed to Malad’s MW Desai Hospital on Thursday with a high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and a headache, only to find that there were zero beds available.Hospital officials say all 39 general beds are packed. Dr Pradnya Malgundkar, the medical superintendent, said most beds are occupied by patients with monsoon illnesses, primarily dengue. “Dengue is on the rise, and patients have low platelets. We do not have enough beds to accommodate them,” she said.Even the 10 ICU beds are fully occupied, split between cardiac patients and severe dengue patients. Rajak’s husband, Sunil, told TOI that they had arrived at the hospital around 3 pm and had to rush Manisha to Jogeshwari Trauma Hospital themselves at their own expense.As per protocol, the hospital was supposed to arrange an ambulance for her.Dr Malgundkar said that the hospital has only one BMC ambulance, which was serving another patient at the time. “We need another ambulance and have already requested an additional 108 ambulance,” she added.City-based gynaecologist Dr Nandita Palshetkar, a former president of the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India (FOGSI), said, “Pregnant women with dengue need to be continuously monitored.”Dr Palshetkar has seen at least two cases like Manisha recently. “In one patient, the platelet count fell to around 30,000. The second patient was carrying twins... one twin suffered an intrauterine fetal death. It is a very distressing situation. Dengue in pregnancy has been associated with foetal distress, pregnancy loss, premature birth, and sometimes risks transmission of the infection to the baby around delivery,” she said.
Article Summary: Mumbai recorded 1,378 cases of dengue in Sept. Doctors report that many of those admitted have critically low platelet counts. “Dengue is on the rise, and patients have low platelets. We do not have enough beds to accommodate them,” says medical superintendent.

Article Title: Where did last year’s Rs 3,000-crore relief package go, Danve asks govt
Article Text:
State govt has yet to clarify the status of the pending assistance or announce a timeline for disbursing fresh aid to the drought-affected farmers

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





Shiv Sena (UBT) MLC Ambadas Danve on Friday slammed BJP-led Mahayuti govt over the alleged non-disbursal of financial aid to drought-hit farmers, questioning the fate of the Rs 3,000-crore relief package announced last year, of which nearly Rs 500 crore in dues allegedly remained unpaid.Raising the issue amid mounting agrarian distress, Danve accused govt of making lofty announcements without ensuring that relief actually reached farmers on the ground. “Govt had announced a Rs 3,000 crore package last year. Where did that package go? Around Rs 500 crore from last year is still pending. This is the question we are raising,” Danve said.The MLC also sought clarity on the assistance planned for farmers affected by the ongoing drought, saying while govt had identified drought-hit talukas, it had yet to spell out the nature or timeline of financial support. “Govt has announced the number of drought-affected talukas. It should now tell farmers what assistance it intends to provide and when,” he said.Danve took a swipe at govt’s handling of the agrarian crisis and said farmers continued to suffer severe financial stress. “Farmers are dying by suicide every day. Such is the grim situation they are facing,” he said.Backing the criticism, All India Kisan Sabha president Rajaj Kshirsagar alleged that farmers reeling from repeated crop losses had been denied timely compensation and support.“Farmers facing successive agricultural setbacks have been seeking timely compensation and financial support to manage mounting losses. But govt is least concerned about the farmers, who are ending their lives unable to bear the stress,” Kshirsagar said.Congress city district president Syed Akram echoed the opposition’s concerns, saying the core issue was the widening gap between govt assurances and the actual delivery of relief. “Danve’s criticism reflects the concerns raised by all opposition parties. We are demanding accountability for pending dues and a clear commitment on fresh relief for farmers,” Akram said.
Article Summary: BJP-led Mahayuti govt slammed over alleged non-disbursal of financial aid to drought-hit farmers. MLC Ambadas Danve questioned fate of Rs 3,000-crore relief package announced last year. Nearly Rs 500 crore in dues allegedly remained unpaid.

Article Title: Raju Shetti demands Rs5,000/tonne initial payout for sugar cane farmers
Article Text:
Kolhapur





: Farmers’ leader and former MP Raju Shetti on Saturday demanded an initial payment of Rs5,000 per tonne for sugar cane for the upcoming crushing season, warning that farmers will prevent mills from starting operations if this demand is not met.Addressing the Swabhimani Shetkari Sanghatana’s (SSS) 25th sugar cane conference in Kolhapur, Shetti said soaring production costs and severe drought have worsened the financial difficulties faced by farmers.“Sugar cane to be crushed this season must receive a first instalment of Rs5,000 per tonne. Production costs have skyrocketed, and sugar cane farmers are in deep trouble due to the drought. In such a situation, farmers must get a fair price for their hard work. Sugar factories must announce this initial payout; otherwise, we will not allow them to start the crushing season,” Shetti warned.He further cautioned that the organisation will indefinitely block national highway traffic at the Kognoli toll booth on the Maharashtra–Karnataka border on October 13 if a favourable decision is not reached during the central government’s scheduled meeting on Oct 12.Additionally, Shetti demanded that the central and state govts provide sugarane growers a subsidy of Rs500 per tonne to compensate for harvesting delays and reduced sugar recovery during transit.He argued that cane harvested after Dec 15 should receive an extra Rs300 per tonne above the fixed rate.Citing widespread crop failures and the acute distress faced by farmers and livestock due to insufficient rainfall, the SSS leader demanded that the state govt deposit drought assistance of Rs1 lakh per hectare directly into the bank accounts of affected farmers. He also sought an increase in the incentive for regular loan repayments under the Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Loan Waiver Scheme, urging it to be raised from Rs50,000 to Rs1 lakh.Turning his focus to industry transparency, Shetti alleged rampant irregularities in weighing, sugar recovery metrics, and stock transactions at sugar mills. He demanded that every factory’s weighing scale be digitised and linked to a transparent online system.He noted that declining ethanol production would heavily burden sugar factories with high interest and instalments on project loans, which would ultimately hurt sugarcane farmers. To mitigate this, he sought a full-year interest subsidy and extended repayment schedules for ethanol project loans.Highlighting that five crore sugar cane farmers and 1.5 lakh workers and agricultural labourers depend entirely on the industry, Shetti demanded a special financial stability policy. He also urged the government to facilitate loans for private and cooperative sugar factories at a concessional 4% annual interest rate through NABARD, the Sugar Development Fund, or the National Cooperative Development Corporation.
Article Summary: Raju Shetti is the leader of Swabhimani Shetkari Sanghatana (SSS) The organisation is holding its 25th sugar cane conference in Kolhapur. Shetti said soaring production costs and severe drought have worsened the financial difficulties faced by farmers.

Article Title: Bananas soaked in ethephon? 1,394kg stock seized in Navi Mumbai raid after video triggers alarm
Article Text:
The inspection revealed that bananas were treated with BTHILEX, which is prohibited for direct use on fruit (Visuals credit: X)





NAVI MUMBAI: Acting on a tip-off, a food safety officer with panch witnesses inspected a stall at APMC Fruit Market, Turbhe, and allegedly found a worker artificially ripening bananas by dipping them in BTHILEX, labelled Ethephon 39% soluble liquid, a plant growth regulator.Officials said the seller claimed he mixed two caps of the chemical in five litres of water.The team seized 1,394kg of bananas, worth about Rs 67,814, stored for sale under Section 38 of the Food Safety and Standards Act , 2006.Three statutory samples of bananas and a surveillance sample of the chemical solution were collected for analysis.Officials said the BTHILEX packaging carried apparently illegitimate manufacturer details, including address, pin code and contact number, and lacked a Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee registration number.FDA officials said the product may be counterfeit or unregistered and is being referred for action under the Insecticides Act, 1968.They said ethephon can only be used to generate ethylene gas; dipping fruit directly in it is prohibited because residues may pose human health risks.
Article Summary: Food safety officer seized 1,394kg of bananas, worth about Rs 67,814. BTHILEX, a plant growth regulator, can only be used to generate ethylene gas. Dipping fruit directly in it is prohibited because residues may pose human health risks.

Article Title: Navi Mumbai Police destroy 726kg narcotics worth Rs 26.30 crore; 3,200 arrested in 5 years
Article Text:
Navi Mumbai police destroyed 726 kgs of narcotics valued at Rs 26.30 crore through incineration





NAVI MUMBAI: Navi Mumbai Police destroyed 726 kg of narcotics worth Rs 26.30 crore that were seized from arrested drug peddlers and suppliers in 201 cases under the NDPS (Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances) Act, 1985, registered at various police stations.The contraband was destroyed on Wednesday at the incineration plant of the government-approved Mumbai Waste Management Company in Taloja, following the legal process and obtaining a court order.Accordingly, till date, the city police have destroyed seized narcotics worth a total of Rs 139.74 crore in 393 NDPS Act cases.In the past five years, police have seized 1,078 kg of narcotics worth around Rs 150 crore and arrested 3,200 accused in 2,378 NDPS Act cases, informed senior inspector Sandeep Nigade of the Anti-Narcotics Cell.SI Nigade said, "In June, the Navi Mumbai police destroyed narcotics collectively worth Rs 56.69 crore that was seized in 26 cases registered under NDPS Act. In March, narcotics collectively worth Rs 18.63 crore that was seized in 55 cases was destroyed. While, in Feb last year, we had destroyed Rs 10 crore worth narcotics seized in 40 drugs peddling cases of contrabands including charas, ganja, MD, MDMA and LSD, which were registered under NDPS Act in 2023 and 2024.Thereafter, Rs 38.45 crore worth drugs seized in 114 cases was destroyed in Sept last year."DCP (Crime) Sachin Gunjal informed, "From 2023 till 2025, a total of 1529 accused African nationals arrested for drugs peddling in the city have been deported and 911 accused African nationals have been blacklisted in the Navi Mumbai Police Commissionerate for illegally staying and selling narcotics. Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act (MOCCA) has been invoked against the accused found repeatedly indulging in drugs trafficking. "Police commissioner Milind Bharambe said, "To make the anti-drugs operation more effective and faster at the local level, a separate 'Anti Narcotics Squad' has been set up at every police station in Navi Mumbai Police Commissionerate.The squad has been assigned the responsibility of collecting local information about drugs peddling, strengthen the network of informants, regular patrolling and inspection at schools, colleges, hotels, lodges, pubs, bars and crime sensitive areas.Also, monitoring of newly emerging drug trends and taking immediate action, scientific investigation and filing of chargesheet in cases registered under NDPS Act.Extensive public awareness programs are being organized in schools, colleges, housing societies and public places. Helpline number '8828-112-112' has already been launched for the citizens to provide any information about drugs peddling and the caller's is kept confidential."
Article Summary: The contraband was destroyed on Wednesday at the incineration plant of the government-approved Mumbai Waste Management Company in Taloja. Till date, the city police have destroyed seized narcotics worth a total of Rs 139.74 crore in 393 NDPS Act cases.

Article Title: Structural defects shut new flyover, commuters heading to Nashik, Gujarat face snarls
Article Text:
With more heavy vehicles, locals say the stretch is now prone to mishaps





THANE: Commuters on the Ghodbunder highway connecting Mumbai, Thane, Navi Mumbai, Nashik and Gujarat continue to face delays, with the Kasarwadavli flyover towards Gaimukh remaining shut for over a month after structural defects were detected last month.The two-lane, one-way flyover, inaugurated in July 2025 to bypass the congested junction, was abruptly closed in September this year after motorists flagged defects in its side barriers. The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) that executed the works subsequently ordered a structural inspection, which reportedly identified multiple issues requiring extensive repairs.The closure has forced Gaimukh-bound freight vehicles onto the adjoining slip road, worsening congestion at the junction. Pedestrians fear the increased movement of heavy vehicles could lead to accidents, while motorists say they lose an average of 20 minutes in each direction while crossing the bottleneck.“Even though travelling on the bridge wasn’t smooth, it helped reduce travel time to some extent. But we never expected it to develop faults so soon. The contractor must be penalised for the inconvenience caused. Crossing the junction is again a nightmare,” said commuter Ashish Shah.Pankaj Shirsat, deputy commissioner of police (traffic), Thane, said the traffic police had received no communication from the MMRDA regarding the flyover’s reopening.The flyover is likely to be repaired and reopen by the end of this month, said the MMRDA, with the contractor likely to bear the cost of inspection and repairs. Details of the defects were however not available while filing this report.The shutdown has also delayed the next phase of the project — a two-lane flyover towards Mumbai, planned in the opposite direction.
Article Summary: The Kasarwadavli flyover towards Gaimukh has been shut for over a month after structural defects were detected last month. The closure has forced freight vehicles onto the adjoining slip road, worsening congestion at the junction. Pedestrians fear the increased movement of heavy vehicles could lead to accidents.

Article Title: Young scientists map Murbad biodiversity amid project row
Article Text:
A group of young scientists is diligently conducting biodiversity surveys to underscore the environmental importance of the area. (Photo credit: Joeanna Fernandes)

Each field visit costs Rs 15,000–20,000, funded largely through donations. (Photo credit: Joeanna Fernandes)

Conflicting assessments

Volunteers believe their data will help challenge what they see as gaps in official impact assessments. (Photo credit: Joeanna Fernandes)

A learning exchange

Two projects and a movement

Kalu Dam:

Location: Kalu river, Murbad taluka, Thane district

Benefits: Dam will supply 1140 MLD to Mumbai region’s cities

Impacts: 2,258.86 ha of land and 18,000 people in Murbad, Thane

Pumped Storage Project

What: A PSP is a type of large-scale water battery that stores and releases electricity on demand, using water and gravity.

Location: Thane and Pune district

Benefits: Supply 1500 MW energy

Impacts: 166.05 ha of land and 2,653 people, company says no one will be displaced

Wildlife impact:

Species count from draft EIA: 273 plants; 27 birds; 14 reptiles; 3 amphibians

Species count on iNaturalist: 468 plants, 154 birds, 34 reptiles; 13 amphibians

Kalu Dam Timeline:

1993: Chitale Committee recommends dam at Kalu

2009: Kalu Dam formally announced

2011: Shramik Mukti Sanghatana files PIL against dam in Bombay HC

2012: HC issues stay on construction work; environment ministry’s forest committee rejects clearance for dam

2013: New forest committee sets aside previous verdict, recommends in-principle clearance

2016: ACB books five engineers from KIDC and partners of FA Enterprises, given work of dam, on charges of cheating and fraud related to the dam.

2020: HC lifts stay, allowing construction to resume

2026: Land acquisition process initiated

2013: New forest committee sets aside previous verdict, recommends in-principal clearance

2016: Five engineers from KIDC and partners of FA Enterprises, booked on charges of cheating and fraudrelated to dam

2020: HC lifts stay

2026: Land acquisition initiated





MURBAD/THANE: Near midnight on a recent Friday, a dozen young men were herded into a pickup truck parked outside Titwala railway station.Around 55 km away, in a bamboo shed doubling as a tribal museum and community centre, a blue tarpaulin awaited them on the earthen floor—their bed for the weekend.Many of the men were strangers to each other, and to Vaishakhare, a village in Murbad where two projects are planned within 10-12 km of each other: the Kalu Dam and the Malshej Ghat Bhorande Pumped Storage Project (PSP), an energy storage plant.Both projects have been opposed by locals who fear displacement or loss of livelihood.The dam, to be built by the Konkan Irrigation Development Corporation (KIDC) and funded by the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), will supply drinking water to Thane, Bhiwandi, Ambernath, and other cities.It is expected to acquire 2,258.86 hectares and impact an estimated 18,000 people. Meanwhile, the 1500 MW PSP, to be built by Adani Renewable Energy Fifty Two Limited, will acquire 166.05 ha and impact at least three villages.Local opposition has recently gained an unlikely ally: young city scientists.For the past year, 20-something botanists, zoologists, and biologists from colleges in Thane, Pune, and Mumbai, have been descending on Kalu and Bhorande, site of the PSP's lower reservoir, to conduct biodiversity surveys and document the community’s ties to the landscape.The aim is to build research-backed evidence of the area’s environmental and cultural significance.“There is no baseline data on the Kalu river and only the People’s Biodiversity Register for Bhorande forest. We need studies robust enough to hold up in court,” says wildlife conservationist Avinash Harad.Initially, they had invited senior scientists to conduct surveys, but their requirements were too costly, he says. So the organisations backing the movement — Shramik Mukti Sanghatana and Ashwamedh Prathisthan—turned to young scientists willing to sleep on a tarp.Each field visit costs Rs 15,000–20,000, funded largely through donations.To date, some 70 researchers have done fieldwork in Murbad, and another 30 have analysed data remotely.“We don't need complex equipment or labs. For most biodiversity studies, photographic evidence is enough,” says Jehu Nadar, a 26-year-old zoologist. He and others hope to publish at least 20 research papers in the coming years.Researchers are not simply counting species but documenting the ties binding people to place: the local Thakar, Mahadeo-Koli and Katkari adivasis — the last classified as a ‘Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group’ — hold traditional rights to forest resources.Volunteers believe their data will help challenge what they see as gaps in official impact assessments.Their data has already thrown up a discrepancy. Around 1,419 species have been logged in the area so far, including 468 plant, 154 bird, 34 reptile and 13 amphibian species.This is more than double the number documented in the draft Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) for the storage project, published this May.Nadar flagged another issue: the 26 fish species listed in the draft EIA were attributed to a 2016 study at an entirely different Kalu Dam in Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar), more than 100 km from here. (The Murbad dam is exempt from an EIA because it is a drinking water project.)In an email response to TOI, a spokesperson for the Adani Group rejected the allegations, saying: "Project assessments indicate no anticipated impact on local flora, fauna, livelihoods, communities or nearby cultural and tourism sites.”The company says it is committed to “environmental safeguards and continued engagement with local communities, while contributing to local infrastructure, livelihoods and regional development."There are also differing claims about people. The draft EIA mentions 2,653 affected people, but the company says this refers simply to the population of the 10-sq-km study area, not the project site.While the project will affect three villages, it will not displace anyone, says the company. However, at least 15 villages have been served public hearing notices by the state pollution control board, says Harad.Nine of them, including Bhorande, have passed resolutions opposing the project.Meanwhile, the gram sabha process for the dam is underway, says Sudarshan Pagar, Executive Director, KIDC, Thane.The land acquisition proposal has been submitted to the district collector's office and the required resolutions will be obtained as per statutory provisions, including PESA, he added.Currently, data on affected houses and families is being collected, Pagar says. Once finalised, a rehabilitation plan will be prepared and submitted to the Divisional Commissioner, Konkan Division, he adds.For some volunteers, the fieldwork has been sobering. "I didn't realise the gravity of the situation until I came here," says Rajas Shrikoli, 24, a marine biologist who signed up expecting a fun excursion.Scientists may be new to the movement, but young people have long been part of it, says Indavi Tulpule, an activist and legal advocate who has led the Kalu agitation for decades. When the dam was first announced in 2009, students from TISS Tuljapur, Nirmala Niketan and colleges in Kalyan helped collect data on potential impacts. Tulpule hopes to deploy research data for any legal battles that might arise. But there are also intangible benefits to the scientific effort.Harad says the presence of city researchers has spurred local youth to engage more deeply with their landscape, potentially opening up work as environmental and cultural guides.The knowledge exchange has run both ways. Under a karanda tree in Bhorande forest, Daulat Pardhi, 29, a guide from the Thakar community, points out a plant curled like a shepherd's crook on the ground, called Gulabdani for its pink flower.When the flowers dry and fall, Pardhi grinds them into powder and uses it to heal wounds. “My mother taught me this,” he says.
Article Summary: The Kalu Dam and the Malshej Ghat Bhorande Pumped Storage Project (PSP) are planned within 10-12 km of each other. Both projects have been opposed by locals who fear displacement or loss of livelihood. Local opposition has recently gained an unlikely ally: young city scientists. They are conducting biodiversity surveys to underscore the environmental importance of the area.

Article Title: Pune: Cameras see activity near Maval watering holes; forest dept plans recharge from Feb, two months early
Article Text:
Birds and animals caught on trap cameras using a watering hole in Pune’s Maval forest

Pune:





With several regions of the state reeling from drought and water shortages, forest officials in Maval said they now plan to start replenishing watering holes for animals from Feb onwards instead of waiting till April, when such interventions are usually carried out.Officials have already identified key watering spots to recharge, thanks to a trap-camera survey that photographed 51 species at natural water sources in the Vadgaon Maval forest range, part of Pune Forest Division. “The survey helped us identify spots most preferred by wildlife for water. Accordingly, we will plan measures to ensure the animals have sufficient water during the summer,” said Range Forest Officer Prakash Shinde.In total, the survey recorded 17 mammal and 34 bird species through 15,581 photographic records. Cameras were installed at eight sites and operated for 30 days at each location.The forest dept usually starts to replenish the watering holes by April or May, when they run dry. But Maval’s below-average rainfall this year has prompted officials to intervene early. The department has also developed nearly 450 artificial water sources for the region’s wildlife.The trap-camera survey documented several mammals of high conservation importance, including Indian leopards and striped hyenas, both listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. Other species recorded included the at-risk rusty-spotted cat, jungle cat, Asian palm civet, small Indian civet and greater false vampire bat. Sambar deer, Indian muntjac, wild boar, primates, mongooses and other small mammals were also documented.The 34 bird species included raptors such as the crested serpent-eagle and shikra, as well as the grey junglefowl and Indian peafowl.The forest around Chikhalse village emerged as the most biodiverse site, recording 28 species — 13 mammals and 15 birds. Other locations surveyed were Paravadi, Akurdi, Kusgaon, Ghorawadi, Aundholi, Apati and Morve villages.Camera data also revealed distinct patterns in the use of water sources. People and livestock mainly accessed them during the day, while wild carnivores and nocturnal mammals visited them at night. This difference in activity times allows different species to use the same water sources with minimal direct interactions.Forest officials said the findings will help prioritise water replenishment, wildlife monitoring and patrolling. Protecting natural water sources from degradation and maintaining habitat connectivity will be crucial to conserving Maval’s biodiversity as temperatures rise and water availability declines, range officer Shinde said.
Article Summary: Officials have already identified key watering spots to recharge, thanks to a trap-camera survey that photographed 51 species. The forest dept usually starts to replenish the watering holes by April or May, when they run dry. But Maval’s below-average rainfall this year has prompted officials to intervene early.
